clinicalPearls: Occurs in the natal cleft over the sacrococcygeal region, presenting with discharge, recurrent swelling, or an acute painful abscess
Characteristic midline pits in the natal cleft, often containing tufts of hair, are the key clinical sign
Predominantly affects young adults, more often men, and is associated with hirsutism, obesity, prolonged sitting, and poor local hygiene
An acute pilonidal abscess is treated by incision and drainage, usually off the midline, to relieve sepsis
Chronic or recurrent disease is managed electively by a range of options from pit-picking and laying open to wide excision with midline or off-midline (flap) closure
Off-midline closure and flap techniques generally give lower recurrence and better healing than midline closure
Recurrence is common, and meticulous hair control and hygiene reduce the risk
Long-standing, non-healing, or atypical sinuses rarely undergo malignant change and should be biopsied if suspicious
reference.pathophysiology: Pilonidal disease is now regarded as an acquired condition in which loose hairs are driven into the skin of the natal cleft, provoking a foreign-body inflammatory reaction and forming midline pits. The pits become epithelialised sinuses that trap further hair and debris, leading to chronic infection, abscess formation, and secondary tracks extending laterally. Friction, sweating, deep natal clefts, hirsutism, and prolonged sitting promote hair insertion and infection. Recurrent cycles of infection and incomplete healing perpetuate the disease.
additionalDifferentials: Anorectal abscess or fistula-in-ano tracking posteriorly
Presacral dermoid or teratoma with sinus
additionalInvestigations: Clinical inspection for midline pits and lateral tracks
Examination to distinguish from anal fistula (relationship to the anal canal)
MRI in complex or recurrent disease or when a deeper or connecting track is suspected
Biopsy of chronic non-healing lesions to exclude malignancy
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis or systemic sepsis from an untreated abscess
A chronic non-healing indurated sinus raising concern for malignant change
Extensive or recurrent disease in an immunosuppressed or diabetic patient
Features suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as anal fistula or Crohn's disease
reference.prognosis: Acute abscesses settle with drainage, but pilonidal disease is prone to recurrence. Definitive excisional and flap-based procedures improve healing and lower recurrence, and long-term outcome is strongly influenced by ongoing hair control and hygiene.
pitfalls: Midline closure of large wounds, which heals poorly and recurs frequently
Mistaking a posteriorly tracking anal fistula for pilonidal disease
Neglecting hair control and hygiene advice, allowing recurrence
Failing to biopsy a chronic non-healing sinus
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Manage an acute pilonidal abscess with incision and drainage, usually off the midline, to relieve sepsis
Treat chronic or recurrent sinus disease electively with options from pit-picking and laying open to wide excision with midline or off-midline flap closure
Favour off-midline and flap techniques, which generally give lower recurrence and better healing than midline closure
Institute ongoing hair control with depilation or laser epilation and improved local hygiene to prevent recurrence
Distinguish from anal fistula clinically and map complex, recurrent or deeper tracks with MRI before definitive surgery
Biopsy chronic non-healing lesions to exclude malignancy
